title: MCP Server
subtitle: Topic: Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server · Subject: Agentic AI · Seven original questions with exact correct answers, realistic distractors, and visual explanations.
hero:
MCP SERVER · AGENTIC AI · VISUAL STUDY

One protocol connects agents to capabilities

Discover tools, read resources, reuse prompts, and call external services through a connected MCP client.

questions.stem: What is an MCP Server in Agentic AI, and how does it help AI agents connect with external tools, applications, and data sources?
options: An MCP Server provides tools, resources, and prompts, but it sends its capabilities straight to the language model without an MCP client; the model then manages each server connection and tool response.

An MCP Server exposes external actions and information through a common interface, but it requires every connected AI host to execute the server's tool code locally rather than sending tool-call requests.
An MCP Server exposes tools, resources, and prompts through a standardized protocol. It allows AI agents to access external information and perform supported actions through connected MCP clients.

An MCP Server publishes tools, resources, and prompts, but clients may only read their descriptions. Agents must separately integrate each application's native API before they can perform any exposed action.
questions.explanation: Explanation: An MCP Server is a program that offers tools, resources, and prompts through Model Context Protocol. An AI application has an MCP client that discovers those capabilities and sends requests to the server. The server can return data or perform an allowed operation; it does not need direct access to the language model. For example, a travel assistant can use a connected calendar server to read event times before suggesting an itinerary. Whether it can modify events depends on the tools and permissions exposed.
questions.technicalExplanation: MCP servers expose distinct tools, resources and prompts. A host's MCP client communicates with a server; the server need not communicate directly with the language model.
questions.figure:
01 · VISUAL LESSON

One bridge to external capabilities

An MCP client mediates access to server capabilities; it is not the same thing as a language model.

questions.stem: Why is the Model Context Protocol needed in Agentic AI, and how does it simplify the integration of different external services?
options: MCP provides a common communication standard between AI applications and external systems. It reduces the need for separate custom integrations and makes tools easier to discover and reuse.

MCP standardizes tool descriptions for AI agents, but each host must still invent a different proprietary request and response format for every server it connects to, making capabilities difficult to reuse.

MCP allows applications to share one tool catalog, but every external service must be rewritten in the same programming language and expose identical internal data structures before integration is possible.

MCP simplifies connecting AI agents by downloading every service's records into the host when it starts. After this initial transfer, tool discovery and remote execution messages are no longer needed.
questions.explanation: Explanation: MCP gives different AI applications a shared way to discover capabilities and exchange requests with external systems. Instead of writing a completely different tool-call protocol for each integration, hosts can use MCP clients to communicate with compatible servers. Each service still needs its own backend implementation, credentials, and access rules. For example, an engineering assistant could connect separately to an issue tracker and documentation system while using the same MCP interaction pattern for both.
questions.technicalExplanation: Standardized MCP methods and message formats reduce per-host integration protocol work. Server implementations, business logic, credentials and service-specific authentication still matter.
questions.figure:
02 · VISUAL LESSON

One protocol, multiple integrations

Services can retain different backends while speaking the same MCP protocol to clients.

questions.stem: What are Tools, Resources, and Prompts in an MCP Server, and what is the purpose of each component?
options: Tools provide read-only data, Resources perform state-changing operations, and Prompts authorize sensitive requests. Together these components let clients work with a server, but their roles are assigned differently.

Tools are reusable instruction templates, Resources expose executable functions, and Prompts supply read-only files. These capabilities help integrate applications, although the three MCP components serve different purposes.

Tools execute server operations, Resources supply accessible information, and Prompts describe which permissions a user owns. This replaces reusable prompt templates with a built-in authorization component on every server.

Tools perform executable operations, Resources provide accessible data, and Prompts offer reusable instruction templates. Together, they help AI applications interact with external systems through MCP.
questions.explanation: Explanation: An MCP tool executes a function, such as looking up an order or submitting a request. A resource exposes information, such as a policy document, for an application to read. A prompt is a reusable template that can guide a conversation. For example, a library server could offer a book-availability tool, a reading-policy resource, and a book-review prompt. These are distinct capabilities: a prompt does not itself execute a tool or grant permission.
questions.technicalExplanation: Tools execute operations; resource URIs provide contextual data; prompts expose reusable templates. Authorization, approval and authentication are separate from these three primitives.
questions.figure:
03 · VISUAL LESSON

Three capabilities, three purposes

Tools run actions, resources supply data, and prompts offer reusable instructions.

questions.stem: How do an MCP Host, MCP Client, and MCP Server communicate when an AI agent needs to discover and execute an external tool?
options: The MCP Host manages the application and sends tool calls directly to external services; the Client only displays tool descriptions, while the Server translates responses after a native API finishes execution.

The MCP Host manages the AI application, the MCP Client communicates with the server, and the MCP Server exposes available tools. The client discovers tools and sends execution requests using MCP messages.
The MCP Host runs the agent, while its Client exposes tools and executes their code. The Server lists available capabilities but does not receive execution requests after discovery is complete.
The MCP Host coordinates an AI application and its Server initiates tool calls when new capabilities appear. The Client accepts these server-initiated actions without first requesting tool execution.
questions.explanation: Explanation: An MCP Host runs the AI application and manages its MCP clients. A client connects to one server, negotiates capabilities, requests the tool list, and sends a tool-call message with arguments. The server validates the request, runs the available function, and returns the result to the client for the host to use. For example, a support agent can discover a ticket-search tool and request the status of a ticket without directly speaking the ticket system's native API.
questions.technicalExplanation: Typical sequence: host starts or connects client, client initializes connection, tools/list discovers tool metadata, tools/call carries arguments to the server, server replies, host consumes result.
questions.figure:
04 · VISUAL LESSON

Discover, call and return

The client discovers available tools before it sends a specific execution request.

questions.stem: How can developers build an MCP Server using Python or JavaScript, register custom tools, and make those tools available to AI agents?
options: Developers create a server with an MCP SDK and register function names, but input schemas are unnecessary because a connected client should guess tool arguments from natural-language descriptions during execution.
Developers implement tools in Python or JavaScript and register them with an SDK, but every AI host must copy the same functions into its own process before clients can discover or call those tools.

Developers use an MCP SDK to create a server, register functions with input schemas, configure a supported transport, and connect an MCP client. The agent can then discover and invoke the registered tools.
Developers use an MCP SDK and select a supported transport, but making a tool discoverable requires placing its function code in an AI model's prompt instead of registering it on the server.
questions.explanation: Explanation: A developer uses the MCP SDK to instantiate a server, decorate or register functions as tools, provide argument types, and choose a transport such as stdio or Streamable HTTP. The SDK exposes tool descriptions and input schemas for a connected client to discover and call. For example, an inventory server could register a read-only `check_stock` tool that accepts a product code. The Python example uses the current SDK interface and starts a local stdio server; deployment also needs appropriate access controls.
questions.technicalExplanation: Python MCP SDK v2: MCPServer constructor registers type-annotated tools; mcp.run() defaults to stdio for local clients; Streamable HTTP is appropriate to remote servers.
questions.figure:
05 · VISUAL LESSON

Register a typed tool with an SDK

Python · MCP SDK v2 Python · 12 lines
from mcp.server import MCPServer

server = MCPServer("Inventory")
STOCK = {"P100": 12, "P200": 0}

@server.tool()
def check_stock(sku: str) -> str:
    """Return available units for this product."""
    return f"{sku}: {STOCK.get(sku, 'unknown')} units"

if __name__ == "__main__":
    server.run()  # stdio by default

Install with pip install 'mcp[cli]'; connect a compatible MCP client to discover check_stock. SDK derives its input schema.

Python MCP SDK v2 uses function type hints to describe tool inputs.

questions.stem: How do JSON-RPC, STDIO, Streamable HTTP, and tool schemas support communication and tool execution between MCP Servers and AI agents?
options: JSON-RPC structures requests and responses, while STDIO and Streamable HTTP provide communication transports. Tool schemas define expected inputs, allowing clients to discover tools, validate arguments, and process execution results.

JSON-RPC supplies message structure and tool calls, while STDIO and Streamable HTTP define separate tool catalogs. Input schemas apply only after execution, so clients cannot check argument shapes before sending requests or interpreting tool errors.

JSON-RPC manages tool requests and results, but STDIO requires a remote web endpoint and Streamable HTTP requires a local subprocess. Tool schemas describe arguments, although their transport roles are reversed.

JSON-RPC encodes messages and STDIO or Streamable HTTP carries them, but tool schemas are optional response summaries rather than definitions of inputs, so clients must infer valid arguments from returned data.
questions.explanation: Explanation: JSON-RPC defines message fields such as `method`, `params`, and `id`. MCP clients can use these messages to list tools or call a named tool with arguments checked against its schema. The transport carries the messages: stdio is common for a local child process, while Streamable HTTP supports remote service endpoints. For example, a stock-check request can send the `sku` argument through either transport and receive a structured tool result. A schema describes valid input, not user authorization.
questions.technicalExplanation: JSON-RPC 2.0 structures protocol messages; stdio uses stdin/stdout for local subprocess communication; Streamable HTTP uses HTTP requests, potentially SSE streaming. Input schema validates form, not identity or authority.
questions.figure:
06 · VISUAL LESSON

Messages travel over two transports

Example · JSON-RPC tool request JSON · 7 lines
{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 7, "method": "tools/call",
  "params": {
    "name": "check_stock",
    "arguments": {"sku": "P100"}
  }
}

Illustrative MCP tools/call request. The client chooses stdio or Streamable HTTP; the server still enforces permissions.

JSON-RPC is the message format. stdio and Streamable HTTP are different ways to carry it.

questions.stem: How can MCP Servers be secured and scaled for production Agentic AI systems while preventing unauthorized tool execution, prompt injection, and sensitive data exposure?
options: Secure MCP Servers inspect inputs and limit request rates, but treat operational directions appearing inside external resource text as trusted server instructions. This avoids separating untrusted data from tool-execution decisions.

Production MCP Servers can use authentication and monitoring, but any authenticated client should be allowed to run all registered tools. Scaling capacity and request logs can replace action-specific authorization checks.

MCP Servers can protect sensitive operations with user approval, but approved requests need no further authorization or input validation. Central credentials and unrestricted tool scopes simplify scaling across many tenants.

Secure MCP Servers use authentication, authorization, input validation, least-privilege permissions, and user approval for sensitive actions. Monitoring, request limits, and scalable infrastructure help maintain reliable operation.
questions.explanation: Explanation: Production MCP Servers need verified identities, per-tool authorization, restricted backend credentials, and validated inputs. Treat external documents and tool outputs as untrusted data: they must not override system instructions or bypass user approval for sensitive actions. Protect secrets, rate-limit expensive calls, log appropriate security events, and scale instances carefully. For example, an internal finance server might allow any employee to read approved reports but require separate authorization and confirmation to initiate payments. Authentication alone is not permission to perform every action.
questions.technicalExplanation: Security layers include authentication, granular tool authorization, approval for sensitive side effects, injection isolation, least-privilege tokens, secret redaction, Origin checks, request quotas, and operational observability.
questions.figure:
07 · VISUAL LESSON

Authorize first, then execute

Permissions, user approval and untrusted-content handling remain essential at production scale.
